outcomes.text: Understand the major stores of water and carbon near Earth's surface and their cycles as systems.

topics.title: 3.1.1.1 Water and carbon cycles as natural systems

outcomes.text: Apply systems ideas to the water and carbon cycles: inputs, outputs, energy, stores, flows, positive and negative feedback, dynamic equilibrium.
Describe the global distribution and size of the major water stores: lithosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere and atmosphere.
Explain processes changing these stores over time and space: evaporation, condensation, cloud formation, causes of precipitation and cryospheric processes at hillslope, basin and global scales.

Explain drainage basins as open systems: precipitation, evapotranspiration, runoff, interception, surface, soil water, groundwater and channel storage, stemflow, infiltration, overland flow and channel flow.
Explain the concept of water balance.
Explain runoff variation and the flood hydrograph.
Explain changes in the water cycle from natural variation (storms, seasons) and human impact (farming, land use change, abstraction).
Describe the global distribution and size of major carbon stores: lithosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, biosphere and atmosphere.
Explain factors changing these stores: photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, combustion, sequestration in oceans and sediments, and weathering.
Explain changes in the carbon cycle from natural variation (wildfires, volcanoes) and human impact (fuel burning, farming, deforestation, land use change).
Explain the carbon budget and the cycle's impact on land, ocean, atmosphere and global climate.

topics.title: 3.1.1.4 Water, carbon, climate and life on Earth

outcomes.text: Explain the role of carbon and water stores and cycles in supporting life, with reference to climate, and the link between them in the atmosphere.
Explain feedbacks within and between cycles, their link to climate change and implications for life.
Describe human interventions in the carbon cycle that aim to influence carbon transfers and reduce climate change effects.

subtopics.title: Skills for water and carbon cycles

outcomes.text: Use simple mass balance, unit conversions, and analysis and presentation of field data.
Study a tropical rainforest setting to analyse water and carbon cycles, environmental change and human activity.
Study a local river catchment using field data to analyse precipitation effects on basin stores and transfers, and implications for water supply or flooding.
Understand hot deserts and margins, their aeolian and episodic fluvial processes and landscapes, using a systems approach.
Apply systems ideas (inputs, outputs, energy, stores, flows, feedback, dynamic equilibrium) and the concepts of landform and landscape.
Describe the global distribution of mid and low latitude arid and semi-arid deserts.
Describe hot desert climate, soils and vegetation and how they interact, with water balance and aridity index.
Explain the causes of aridity: pressure, winds, continentality, relief and cold ocean currents.
Describe energy sources in deserts: insolation, winds and runoff, and sediment sources, cells and budgets.
Explain weathering, mass movement, erosion, transportation and deposition, and distinctively arid weathering (thermal fracture, exfoliation, chemical, block and granular disintegration).
Explain wind erosion (deflation, abrasion), transport (suspension, saltation, creep) and deposition.
Explain water sources (exogenous, endoreic, ephemeral) and the episodic role of sheet flooding and flash floods.

topics.title: 3.1.2.3 Arid landscape development in contrasting settings

outcomes.text: Explain aeolian landforms: deflation hollows, desert pavements, ventifacts, yardangs, zeugen, barchans and seif dunes.
Explain water-formed landforms: wadis, bahadas, pediments, playas and inselbergs.
Relate process, time, landforms and landscapes in characteristic desert landscapes.
Describe the changing extent of hot deserts over the last 10,000 years.
Explain causes of desertification (climate change, human impact), areas at risk and impacts on ecosystems, landscapes and people.
Explain predicted climate change impacts and possible futures for local populations.
Use quantitative and qualitative skills: observation, measurement, geospatial mapping, data manipulation and statistics on field measurements.
Study a hot desert environment with field data, possibly coastal dunes as an analogue.
Study a local landscape where desertification has occurred, evaluating resilience, mitigation and adaptation and sustainable development.
Understand coastal zones where winds, waves, currents and sediments shape landscapes, using a systems approach.
Apply systems ideas (inputs, outputs, energy, stores, flows, feedback, dynamic equilibrium) and the concepts of landform and landscape.
Describe energy sources: winds, constructive and destructive waves, currents and tides, and low and high energy coasts.
Describe sediment sources, cells and budgets.
Explain weathering, mass movement, erosion, transportation and deposition.
Explain marine erosion (hydraulic action, quarrying, abrasion, cavitation, solution, attrition), transport (traction, suspension, longshore drift), and sub-aerial processes.
Explain landforms of coastal erosion: cliffs, wave-cut platforms, caves, arches and stacks.
Explain landforms of coastal deposition: beaches, spits, tombolos, offshore bars, barrier beaches and islands, sand dunes.
Explain estuarine mudflat and saltmarsh environments and how they develop.
Explain eustatic, isostatic and tectonic sea level change and major changes in the last 10,000 years.
Explain coastlines of emergence and submergence: raised beaches, marine platforms, rias, fjords, Dalmatian coasts.
Explain recent and predicted climate change and its potential impact on coasts.
Relate process, time, landforms and landscapes in coastal settings, including landscapes beyond the UK.
Explain human intervention and traditional hard and soft engineering for flood and erosion risk.
Explain sustainable approaches: shoreline management and integrated coastal zone management.
Use quantitative and qualitative skills: observation, measurement, geospatial mapping, data manipulation and statistics on field measurements.
Study a local coast with field data, analysing processes, landscapes and sustainable management challenges.
Study a contrasting coast beyond the UK, evaluating risks, opportunities and resilience, mitigation and adaptation.
Understand glaciated landscapes shaped by contemporary processes and Pleistocene conditions, using a systems approach.
Apply systems ideas (inputs, outputs, energy, stores, flows, feedback, dynamic equilibrium) and the concepts of landform and landscape.

topics.title: 3.1.4.2 The nature and distribution of cold environments

outcomes.text: Describe the global distribution of cold environments.
Describe the climate, soils and vegetation of cold environments and how they interact.
Describe past and present polar, alpine, glacial and periglacial environments and areas of Pleistocene glaciation.
Explain glacial systems and budgets, ablation and accumulation, and historical ice advance and retreat.
Compare warm-based and cold-based glaciers.
Explain frost action, nivation, ice movement types, plucking, abrasion, transportation and deposition.
Explain fluvioglacial processes of meltwater erosion, transport and deposition.
Explain periglacial processes: permafrost, active layer and mass movement.
Explain erosional landforms: corries, arêtes, glacial troughs, hanging valleys, truncated spurs, roches moutonnées.
Explain depositional landforms: drumlins, erratics, moraines and till plains.
Explain fluvioglacial landforms: meltwater channels, kames, eskers and outwash plains.
Explain periglacial landforms: patterned ground, ice wedges, pingos, blockfields, solifluction lobes, terracettes, thermokarst.
Relate process, time, landforms and landscapes in glaciated and periglacial settings, including beyond the UK.
Explain environmental fragility and human impacts on cold environments over time and scale.
Explain impacts of climate change and the management of cold environments now and in possible futures.
Use quantitative and qualitative skills: observation, measurement, geospatial mapping, data manipulation and statistics on field measurements.
Study a local glaciated environment with field data, analysing glacial processes and landscapes.
Study a contrasting glaciated landscape beyond the UK, evaluating challenges, opportunities and resilience, mitigation and adaptation.
Understand lithospheric and atmospheric natural hazards and how people respond (optional topic).

topics.title: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

outcomes.text: Describe geophysical, atmospheric and hydrological hazards and their potential impacts.
Explain hazard perception and its economic and cultural determinants.
Explain human responses (fatalism, prediction, adaptation, mitigation, management, risk sharing) and how they relate to hazard type and development level.
Use the Park model of human response and the Hazard Management Cycle.
Describe Earth's structure and internal energy sources.
Explain plate movement: gravitational sliding, ridge push, slab pull, convection currents and sea-floor spreading.
Describe destructive, constructive and conservative margins, with seismicity and vulcanicity.
Explain landforms: fold mountains, rift valleys, ocean ridges, trenches, island arcs, volcanoes, and magma plumes.
Explain vulcanicity and plate tectonics, and hazard forms: nuées ardentes, lava, mudflows, ash fallout, gases, tephra.
Explain spatial distribution, magnitude, frequency and predictability of volcanic events.
Explain primary and secondary impacts and responses: preparedness, mitigation, prevention, adaptation.
Study impacts and responses in a recent volcanic event.
Explain seismicity and plate tectonics, and hazard forms: earthquakes, shockwaves, tsunamis, liquefaction, landslides.
Explain spatial distribution, magnitude, frequency and predictability of seismic events.
Explain primary and secondary impacts and responses.
Study impacts and responses in a recent seismic event.
Explain tropical storms and their causes, and hazard forms: high winds, storm surges, coastal and river flooding, landslides.
Explain distribution, magnitude, frequency and predictability of storms.
Explain primary and secondary impacts and responses.
Study impacts and responses in two recent tropical storms in contrasting areas.
Explain wildfires and conditions favouring intense fires: vegetation, fuel, climate, weather and fire behaviour.
Explain natural and human causes of fires.
Explain impacts and responses, using a recent wildfire event.
Study a multi-hazard environment beyond the UK, including resilience, adaptation, mitigation and management.
Study a local hazardous place, analysing how its community reflects the hazard and its response.
Understand ecosystems and how human activity and population growth stress them (optional topic).
Explain biodiversity, local and global trends, and causes, rates and impacts of its decline.
Explain why ecosystems matter to growing human populations and their role in sustainability.
Describe ecosystem structure, energy flows, trophic levels, food chains and food webs.
Apply systems concepts, biomass and net primary production to ecosystems.
Explain succession: seral stages, climatic climax, sub-climax and plagioclimax, and mineral nutrient cycling.
Explain how climate, vegetation, soil and topography interconnect in terrestrial ecosystems.
Explain ecosystem responses to changes in components and factors changing them, including climate change and human exploitation.
Explain the biome concept and global distribution of major terrestrial biomes.
Compare tropical rainforest and savanna: characteristics, climate and soil adaptations, human impact and development issues.

topics.title: 3.1.6.4 Ecosystems in the British Isles over time

outcomes.text: Explain succession and climatic climax with lithoseres and hydroseres.
Describe the temperate deciduous woodland climax.
Explain human effects on succession, illustrated by a plagioclimax such as heather moorland.
Describe coral reef distribution, characteristics and the conditions for reef development.
Explain, for a named reef, natural and human factors in reef health: temperature, acidity, salinity, algal blooms, drainage schemes, development, pollution, tourism, fishing.
Assess future prospects for coral reefs.
Describe a distinctive local ecosystem and its flora and fauna adaptations to climate, soil and moisture.
Explain local factors of ecological change such as agriculture, urban change and introduced species.
Explain impacts of change, management measures and conservation strategies in specific settings.
Study a region experiencing ecological change: reasons, community character and response.
Study a local ecosystem: its properties, human impact and sustainable development challenges.
Use interviews and a mixture of methods, and interpret and evaluate text and visual sources.
Explain the opportunities and limits of qualitative techniques such as coding and sampling, and how they create geographical representations.
Explain the ethical and socio-political implications of collecting and representing data about communities.
Explain what makes data geographical, including GIS, and collect and use digital and geo-located data.
Use descriptive statistics, measures of difference and association, inferential statistics, measurement, errors and sampling.
Question data sources, spot error and misuse, and communicate evidence-based conclusions in extended argument.
Use and annotate base maps, sketch maps, OS maps, diagrams, graphs, field sketches, photographs and digital imagery, with overlays.
Use literacy and coding with text, numeracy and measurement, and questionnaire and interview techniques.
Use atlas maps, weather maps and synoptic charts, and maps with proportional symbols.
Use maps showing movement (flow, desire and trip lines) and spatial patterns (choropleth, isoline, dot).
Draw line and bar graphs (simple, comparative, compound, divergent), scatter graphs with best fit lines, and pie charts and divided circles.
Draw triangular graphs, graphs with logarithmic scales, and dispersion diagrams.
Calculate measures of central tendency (mean, mode, median) and dispersion (range, interquartile range, standard deviation).
Apply Spearman's rank correlation, Chi-square tests and significance tests.
Use remotely sensed data, electronic databases and crowd-sourced or big data.
Use ICT to produce maps, graphs and statistical calculations.
Understand globalisation, international trade and the governance of the global commons.
Describe dimensions of globalisation: flows of capital, labour, products, services and information, global marketing, and patterns of production, distribution and consumption.
Explain factors in globalisation: technologies, financial, transport, security, communications, management and information systems, and trade agreements.
Describe the economic, political, social and environmental interdependence of the contemporary world.
Explain how unequal flows of people, money, ideas and technology can promote growth yet cause inequalities, conflicts and injustices.
Explain how unequal power relations let some states drive global systems and others only respond or resist.

topics.title: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

outcomes.text: Describe global trends in the volume and pattern of international trade and investment.
Compare trading relationships among developed economies (US, EU), emerging economies (China, India) and smaller economies (sub-Saharan Africa, southern Asia, Latin America).
Explain differential access to markets by development level and trading agreements, and effects on well-being.
Explain the role of transnational corporations: spatial organisation, production, linkages, trading and marketing, with a specified TNC and its impacts.
Study world trade in at least one food commodity or manufacturing product.
Assess how trade and variable market access affect people's lives across the globe.
Explain the emergence of norms, laws and institutions regulating global systems.
Explain how agencies such as the post-1945 UN can promote stability and growth but also worsen inequalities.
Explain how interactions among local, regional, national, international and global scales shape governance.
Explain the global commons, everyone's rights to its benefits, and the need to balance sustainable development with protecting it.
Outline Antarctica's geography and climate, its role as a global common and its vulnerability to economic pressure and environmental change.
Explain threats: climate change, fishing and whaling, mineral resource search, tourism and scientific research.
Appraise governance: UNEP, International Whaling Commission, Antarctic Treaty 1959, Environmental Protocol 1991, whaling moratorium 1982, with inspection and enforcement.
Explain the role of NGOs in monitoring threats and protecting Antarctica.
Assess how global governance affects citizens and places in Antarctica and elsewhere.
Weigh the benefits of growth, development, integration and stability against inequality, injustice, conflict and environmental costs.
Use quantitative and qualitative approaches across the theme.
Understand how people engage with places and how places change, through a local and a contrasting place.

topics.title: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

outcomes.text: Explain the concept of place, its importance to human experience, and insider and outsider perspectives.
Distinguish near and far places, experienced and media places.
Explain endogenous factors of place character (location, physical geography, land use, built environment, demographics, economy) and exogenous ones (relationships with other places).

topics.title: 3.2.2.2 Changing places - relationships, connections, meaning and representation

outcomes.text: Explain how relationships and connections, and meaning and representation, affect continuity and change in a local place and a contrasting place at all scales.
Explain how continuity and change in places affect students' lives and others'.

Explain how shifting flows of people, resources, money, investment and ideas shape the demographic, socio-economic and cultural character of places, focusing on either demographic and cultural change or economic change and inequalities.
Explain external forces at different scales: government policy, transnational corporations or international institutions.
Explain how past and present connections embed places in wider scales.
Explain how people perceive, form attachments to and represent places, and how place meanings tie to identities.
Explain how governments, corporations and community groups try to create place meanings and shape behaviour.
Explain how places are represented in advertising, tourism, film, photography, art and song, contrasting with maps and census data.
Explain how past and present development processes shape present place meanings.
Use quantitative and geospatial data to present place characteristics, and critically analyse media influence on place meanings.
Study a local place's developing character and a contrasting distant place, using past and present qualitative and quantitative data.
Focus equally on lived experience and either demographic and cultural change or economic change and inequality.
Use sources such as census data, maps, GIS, photographs, media, artistic works and oral sources.
Understand urban growth and change and the challenges of sustainability and social cohesion (optional topic).
Describe global urbanisation since 1945: urbanisation, suburbanisation, counter-urbanisation, urban resurgence, megacities and world cities.
Explain economic, social, technological, political and demographic processes driving urban growth.
Explain urban change: deindustrialisation, decentralisation, service economy growth, and urban policy and regeneration in Britain since 1979.
Describe mega and world city characteristics and urban characteristics in contrasting settings.
Explain spatial patterns of land use, inequality, segregation and diversity, and their causes.
Describe new urban landscapes: mixed town centres, cultural quarters, fortress developments, gentrification, edge cities, and the post-modern western city.

topics.title: 3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation

outcomes.text: Explain economic inequality, social segregation and cultural diversity in contrasting urban areas.
Evaluate strategies to manage these issues.
Explain the urban heat island effect and urban effects on precipitation, fogs and thunderstorms.
Explain the effects of urban structure on wind.
Explain air quality, particulate and photochemical pollution, and pollution reduction policies.
Explain urban precipitation, surfaces and catchments, effects on basin storage and the urban water cycle through hydrographs.
Explain urban catchment management issues and sustainable urban drainage systems.
Study a river restoration project: reasons, aims, parties' attitudes, activities and outcomes.
Explain sources of urban waste and how waste streams relate to economy, lifestyle and attitudes.
Explain environmental impacts of waste disposal options: unregulated, recycling, recovery, incineration, burial, submergence, trade.
Compare incineration and landfill for a specified urban area.
Explain atmospheric pollution, water pollution and dereliction in contrasting urban areas.
Evaluate strategies to manage these problems.
Explain urban impacts on local and global environments and the ecological footprint of major cities.
Explain dimensions of sustainability (natural, physical, social, economic), features of sustainable cities and liveability.
Evaluate opportunities, challenges and strategies for more sustainable cities.
Study two contrasting urban areas: economic and social well-being, physical environmental conditions, and implications for sustainability, character and residents' attitudes.
Understand links between physical environment, population, health and development (optional topic).
Describe key physical environment elements (climate, soils, resources including water) and population parameters (distribution, density, numbers, change).
Describe global patterns of population numbers, densities and change rates and the role of development.
Describe global and regional patterns of food production and consumption, agricultural systems and productivity.
Explain how two climatic types relate to human activity and numbers, and how climate change affects agriculture.
Explain how two zonal soils relate to agriculture and soil problems: erosion, waterlogging, salinisation, structural deterioration.
Evaluate strategies for food security.
Describe global patterns of health, mortality and morbidity and the epidemiological transition.
Relate environmental variables, air quality and water quality to disease incidence.
Study one biologically transmitted disease (such as malaria): distribution, links to environments and vectors, impacts and management.
Study one non-communicable disease: distribution, links to environment and lifestyle, impacts and management.
Explain the role of international agencies and NGOs in global health.
Explain natural population change: demographic transition model, vital rates, age-sex composition, cultural controls, and the demographic dividend.
Explain international migration by refugees, asylum seekers and economic migrants: causes, processes and implications.

topics.title: 3.2.4.5 Principles of population ecology and their application to human populations

outcomes.text: Explain population growth dynamics, overpopulation, underpopulation and optimum population.
Explain carrying capacity, ecological footprint and the population, resources and pollution model with feedback.
Compare Malthusian, neo-Malthusian, Boserup and Simon perspectives.
Explain health impacts of global change: ozone depletion, climate change and vector-borne disease, agricultural productivity, nutrition.
Appraise projected global population and future population-environment relationships.
Study a country or society with population increase or decline, its factors and implications.
Study a local area on place and health, linked to physical environment, socio-economic character and residents' experience.
Understand the exploitation of unevenly distributed water, energy and mineral resources (optional topic).
Explain resources, stock and flow classifications, and stock evaluation: measured, indicated, inferred and possible.
Explain resource development over time, the resource frontier and resource peak.
Explain sustainable resource development and Environmental Impact Assessment.
Describe global patterns of production, consumption and trade of energy and ore minerals.
Describe global patterns of water availability and demand.
Explain the geopolitics of energy, ore and water distribution, trade and management.
Explain sources of water, demand components, water stress, and links to climate, geology and drainage.
Evaluate strategies to increase supply: catchment, diversion, storage, transfers, desalination.
Explain environmental impacts of a major water scheme with a dam or barrage.
Evaluate strategies to manage consumption and cut demand.
Explain sustainability issues: virtual water, conservation, recycling, greywater and groundwater management.
Explain water conflicts at local, national and international scales.
Describe primary and secondary energy sources, demand components and energy mixes in contrasting settings.
Relate energy supply to climate, geology and drainage.
Explain competing national interests and the role of transnational corporations in energy production, processing and distribution.
Explain environmental impacts of a major energy development such as an oil, coal or gas field.
Evaluate strategies to raise supply: exploration, nuclear power, renewables.
Evaluate strategies to manage consumption and cut demand.
Explain sustainability issues: acid rain, enhanced greenhouse effect, nuclear waste, energy conservation.
Study a globally traded ore such as iron ore, copper, tin or manganese: sources, reserves, end uses, demand and role in industry.
Relate ore occurrence and working to geological conditions and location.
Explain environmental impacts of a major mineral extraction scheme and its distribution networks.
Explain sustainability issues in ore extraction, trade and processing.
Evaluate alternative energy, water and ore futures and their links to technological, economic, environmental and political developments.
Study a water, energy or mineral issue in a global or regional setting: implications, resource security and human welfare, and management.
Study a place whose physical environment affects the availability, cost and use of water, energy or ore.
Undertake four days of fieldwork on both physical and human geography processes, locally or further afield.
Carry out an independent investigation with a significant fieldwork element, human, physical or both, using individual or group-collected data.
Define a research question or hypothesis tied to the specification, and research the literature and its theoretical or comparative context.
Observe and record good-quality field data and justify the approach: timing, sampling and data collection.
Choose and apply suitable quantitative or qualitative techniques to analyse and represent results.
Critically examine data for accuracy and representativeness and extend geographical understanding.
Contextualise, analyse and summarise findings, apply theory and draw conclusions.
Write up results clearly with varied presentation methods and extended writing, answering a specific geographical question with evidence and theory.
Evaluate the investigation, including ethical dimensions of field research.
Write a report of 3,000-4,000 words with a manageable focus, a theoretical basis and a locational context.
Work independently on defining the question, drawing on research, analysing and summarising data, and presenting and concluding.
Collaborate only to explore the investigation's focus and collect field data.
